question: Why and how well does sampling an environment from the posterior and playing its optimal action explore, in finite-armed, linear and adversarial-Bayesian bandits?
contributions: Bayesian regret O(sqrt(kn log n)) for finite-armed Thompson sampling via the UCB proof (Thm 36.1)
Frequentist play-count bound for follow-the-perturbed-leader and asymptotic optimality for Gaussian bandits (Thm 36.2, 36.3)
Information-theoretic analysis giving sqrt(kn log(k)/2) for Bayesian adversarial bandits (Thm 36.5-36.6)

limits: Frequentist theorems are for Gaussian (realisable) rewards; Agrawal and Goyal prove bounds for rewards in [0,1] (p474).
Frequentist analysis for linear bandits requires inflating the posterior variance by Theta(d), losing sqrt(d) vs LinUCB (Note 6).
Linear Thompson sampling is not asymptotically optimal; conditions for Thompson sampling being close to optimal remain an open challenge (Note 2).
Gaussian Thompson sampling is not minimax optimal (Note 3); Experiment 36.1 shows larger regret and variance than AdaUCB.
Information-theoretic technique gives Bayesian bounds, not algorithms for the adversarial setting (Note 11).
Authors say what randomisation gains or loses in Thompson sampling is still not clear (p460).
Experiment 36.1 is a single two-armed instance; Exercise 36.14(c) asks the reader to test other bandits. Constant C unspecified in Thm 36.1 and 36.3.
practices: Choose the prior with care: a prior that underestimates an arm can leave it unplayed forever, unlike classical Bayesian statistics where data washes the prior away (Note 5, p472).

For linear bandits with Gaussian prior and known-variance Gaussian noise, sample theta_t from the posterior and take a linear argmax; this avoids LinUCB's inner max over the confidence set (Sec 36.3.1).
In practice r = 1 in the linear Thompson sampler often performs well, though the theory needs r = Theta(d) (Note 6).
Consider BayesUCB (posterior quantile as upper confidence bound) as an alternative with strong empirical and theoretical guarantees (Note 4, p472).
In non-Bayesian structured problems cheaper exploration than posterior sampling may exist (Note 1, p471).

terms.definition: the learner chooses a prior over bandit environments, samples an environment from the posterior each round and acts optimally for it
(a) pick arm with posterior probability that it is optimal; (b) sample environment from posterior, play its optimal action; (c) with independent arms, sample each arm's mean and take the largest
sample theta_i(t) ~ F_i(t) independently per arm, play argmax; only the played arm's F is updated; Thompson sampling is the case F_i = posterior of arm mean under a product prior
BR_n = E[sum_t (mu_A* - mu_At)], expectation also over the prior
sample A_t from the P_t minimising squared expected regret over expected information gain about A*
